text: If you've only worked in one cloud so far, adding AWS on top sounds like doubling your job. It isn't — because the hard part of cloud security was never the specific product name, it was the underlying primitive: identity, policy enforcement, network boundaries, and logging. Every cloud has to solve those same problems. Once you see that, a second cloud becomes translation, not re-learning from zero.

Treat the mapping as a Rosetta Stone. Entra ID and AWS IAM both answer 'who can do what.' Management groups and subscriptions mirror AWS Organizations, OUs, and accounts. Azure Policy and AWS Config plus Service Control Policies both enforce rules at scale. Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AWS Security Hub both score your posture. Azure Monitor and AWS CloudTrail both centralize your logs. One requirement — did we enforce MFA for privileged accounts — just has two implementations.

The real extra cost isn't duplicating controls — it's three specific things. First, scope translation: a subscription and an AWS account aren't quite the same isolation boundary, and getting that wrong means applying a policy at the wrong level. Second, federated identity: most real dual-cloud shops federate AWS to Entra ID as the single source of truth rather than running two identity stores. Third, log and alert aggregation, which is the single biggest lever for making two clouds feel like one job.

CIS publishes a separate benchmark for Azure and for AWS, but both exist to enforce the same control intent. Require MFA for privileged roles, and on Azure that's a Conditional Access policy in Entra ID; on AWS it's an IAM policy backed by an SCP guardrail, or a permission set in IAM Identity Center. You pick the framework once. You implement it twice. You do not redesign the security program twice.

This is exactly why Microsoft Defender for Cloud now treats AWS as a first-class environment, not an afterthought. Connect an AWS account, and its CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark findings, its GuardDuty alerts, and its Security Hub findings land in the same secure score and the same recommendations view you already use for Azure.

That's the architecture this course assumes from here forward: not two security programs running in parallel, but one program operated against two sets of native APIs, with a unifying posture layer collapsing the view back down to one. Next lesson takes that shared control intent and turns it into an actual baseline, built from real CIS Benchmarks for both clouds.
